notes.front: What is Microsoft Purview?
notes.back: A family of Microsoft solutions for governing, protecting and managing an organisation's data, wherever that data is kept.
notes.explanation: It brings together insight into data held on premises, in several clouds and in software-as-a-service apps, giving one unified view.
notes.example: Like a library's catalogue and security desk combined, but covering every place the organisation keeps information.
notes.source: Microsoft Purview documentation: Learn about Microsoft Purview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure Policy?
notes.back: An Azure service that enforces organisational standards on resources and assesses compliance at scale.
notes.explanation: Its compliance dashboard gives an overall view of the environment that you can drill into per resource and per policy.
notes.example: Like a building code inspector who checks every new build against the rules, but for Azure resource settings.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “What is Azure Policy?”
notes.evidence: This overview describes how Azure Policy helps to enforce organizational standards and to assess compliance at-scale. Through its compliance dashboard, it provides an aggregated view to evaluate the overall state of the environment, with the ability to drill down to the per-resource, per-policy granularity.

notes.front: What is a policy initiative in Azure Policy?
notes.back: A collection of policy definitions grouped to achieve one overarching goal.
notes.explanation: Grouping the policies as one item makes them simpler to manage and assign.
notes.example: Like a fire-safety checklist that bundles separate rules on exits, alarms and extinguishers under one inspection.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “Initiative definition”
notes.evidence: An initiative definition is a collection of policy definitions that are tailored toward achieving a singular overarching goal. Initiative definitions simplify managing and assigning policy definitions. They simplify by grouping a set of policies as one single item.

notes.front: What is a resource lock in Azure?
notes.back: A lock on a subscription, resource group or resource that protects it from accidental deletion or modification.
notes.explanation: The lock overrides any user permissions, so even people allowed to delete or change the item are stopped.
notes.example: Like a padlock on a server cabinet that even the building manager must open before touching anything inside.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure
notes.evidence: As an administrator, you can lock an Azure subscription, resource group, or resource to protect them from accidental user deletions and modifications. The lock overrides any user permissions.

notes.front: What does a CanNotDelete lock do?
notes.back: Authorised users can still read and modify the resource but can't delete it. The portal calls it a Delete lock.
notes.explanation: The same two locks have different names in the Azure portal and on the command line.
notes.example: Like a museum exhibit label you may rewrite, fixed to a case that can't be taken away.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure
notes.evidence: In the portal, these locks are called **Delete** and **Read-only**. In the command line, these locks are called **CanNotDelete** and **ReadOnly**. - **CanNotDelete** means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it.

notes.front: What does a ReadOnly lock do?
notes.back: Authorised users can read the resource but can't delete or update it. The portal calls it a Read-only lock.
notes.explanation: Applying it is similar to limiting every authorised user to what the Reader role allows.
notes.example: Like a signed contract in a glass case: anyone may read it, nobody may alter or remove it.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure
notes.evidence: **ReadOnly** means authorized users can read a resource, but they can't delete or update it. Applying this lock is similar to restricting all authorized users to the permissions that the **Reader** role provides.

notes.front: What is the Microsoft Service Trust Portal?
notes.back: A Microsoft portal of content, tools and resources about Microsoft's security, privacy and compliance practices.
notes.explanation: It details the controls and processes Microsoft uses to protect its cloud services and customer data.
notes.example: Like a supplier's audit reading room, where customers can inspect certificates and reports before signing up.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the purpose of the Service Trust portal
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Azure Policy compare resources against when it evaluates them?
notes.back: Business rules called policy definitions.
notes.explanation: The definitions are written in a structured text format, and several can be grouped into an initiative.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “Overview”
notes.evidence: Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules. These business rules, described in JSON format, are known as policy definitions. To simplify management, several business rules can be grouped together to form a policy initiative

notes.front: Besides reacting to changes, how often does Azure Policy run its standard compliance evaluation?
notes.back: Once every 24 hours.
notes.explanation: Evaluation also happens when a resource is created or updated in scope, or when an assignment is added or updated.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “Understand evaluation outcomes”
notes.evidence: A resource is created or updated in a scope with a policy assignment. - A scope gets a new assignment of a policy or initiative. - A policy or initiative already assigned to a scope is updated. - The standard compliance evaluation cycle that occurs once every 24 hours.

notes.front: What are two governance actions you can enforce with Azure Policy?
notes.back: Any two, among others: deploy resources only to allowed regions; apply tags consistently.
notes.explanation: Built-in policy definitions for common uses such as these already exist in every Azure environment.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “What is Azure Policy?”
notes.evidence: Policy definitions for these common use cases are already available in your Azure environment as built-ins to help you get started. Some useful governance actions you can enforce with Azure Policy include: - Ensure your team deploys Azure resources only to allowed regions. - Enforce the consistent application of taxonomic tags.

notes.front: When a policy is assigned to a management group or subscription, which resources does it cover?
notes.back: All resources within that scope, though subscopes can be excluded if necessary.
notes.explanation: An assignment can be made at any supported scope, from a management group down to one resource, and flows down from there.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “Overview”
notes.evidence: After your business rules are formed, the policy definition or initiative is assigned to any scope of resources that Azure supports. For example, management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, or individual resources. The assignment applies to all resources within the Resource Manager scope of that assignment. Subscopes can be excluded, if necessary.

notes.front: How can Azure Policy bring resources into compliance?
notes.back: Through bulk remediation of existing resources and automatic remediation of new ones.
notes.explanation: Remediation covers resources already deployed as well as resources created later.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “What is Azure Policy?”
notes.evidence: It also helps to bring your resources to compliance through bulk remediation for existing resources and automatic remediation for new resources.

notes.front: The Azure Policy documentation's example initiative monitors all the security recommendations of which service? (Older training material calls it Azure Security Center.)
notes.back: Microsoft Defender for Cloud.
notes.explanation: Its goal is to track all the available security recommendations as one grouped item.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “Initiative definition”
notes.evidence: For example, you could create an initiative titled **Enable Monitoring in Microsoft Defender for Cloud**, with a goal to monitor all the available security recommendations in your Microsoft Defender for Cloud instance.

notes.front: How does Azure Policy differ from Azure role-based access control?
notes.back: Azure Policy checks that resource state complies with rules, whoever made the change; role-based access control manages what users may do.
notes.explanation: Even a user allowed to perform an action is still blocked by Azure Policy if the result would be a noncompliant resource.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “Azure Policy and Azure RBAC”
notes.evidence: Azure RBAC focuses on managing user actions at different scopes. If control of an action is required based on user information, then Azure RBAC is the correct tool to use. Even if an individual has access to perform an action, if the result is a non-compliant resource, Azure Policy still blocks the create or update.

notes.front: You lock a resource group. What happens to resources you add to it later?
notes.back: They inherit the same lock; the most restrictive lock in the chain takes precedence.
notes.explanation: A lock at a parent scope applies to every resource within it, including resources added afterwards.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure, “Lock inheritance”
notes.evidence: When you apply a lock at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit the same lock. Even resources you add later inherit the same parent lock. The most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence.

notes.front: Can the Owner of a locked resource carry out the action the lock blocks?
notes.back: Not until the lock is removed: locks apply whatever role-based permissions a user holds.
notes.explanation: Changing a locked resource is a two-step process: remove the lock, then perform any action your permissions allow.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the purpose of resource locks, “How do I delete or change a locked resource?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does a ReadOnly lock on a database server stop users creating, updating or deleting data in its databases?
notes.back: No. Locks apply only to control plane (management) operations, not to data plane operations.
notes.explanation: Locks protect a resource from changes but don't restrict how it performs its functions.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure, “Understand scope of locks”
notes.evidence: The distinction means locks protect a resource from changes, but they don't restrict how a resource performs its functions. For example, a ReadOnly lock on an SQL Database logical server protects it from deletions or modifications. It allows you to create, update, or delete data in the server database.

notes.front: Applying a ReadOnly lock is similar to limiting every authorised user to the permissions of which built-in role?
notes.back: The Reader role.
notes.explanation: Unlike a role assignment, a lock applies the restriction across all users and roles at once.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure
notes.evidence: Applying this lock is similar to restricting all authorized users to the permissions that the **Reader** role provides. Unlike with role-based access control (RBAC), you use management locks to apply a restriction across all users and roles.

notes.front: What can authorised users still do to a resource under a CanNotDelete lock that they can't do under a ReadOnly lock?
notes.back: Modify (update) it. Both locks allow reading and both prevent deletion.
notes.explanation: CanNotDelete blocks only deletion, while ReadOnly blocks both deletion and updates.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure
notes.evidence: **CanNotDelete** means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it. - **ReadOnly** means authorized users can read a resource, but they can't delete or update it.

notes.front: What must you do to open some of the Service Trust Portal's compliance materials?
notes.back: Sign in with a Microsoft cloud services (work or school) account and accept Microsoft's non-disclosure agreement.
notes.explanation: Some content is open, but some resources are only for authenticated users.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the purpose of the Service Trust portal
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When does Azure Blueprints (Preview) retire?
notes.back: On 31 January 2027, after a phased retirement that began on 31 July 2026.
notes.explanation: Microsoft asks users to move blueprint definitions and assignments to deployment stacks (recommended) and template specs before that date.
notes.source: Azure Blueprints documentation: Overview of Azure Blueprints, “Azure Blueprints retirement”
notes.evidence: Azure Blueprints (Preview) is being retired on **January 31, 2027**, with a phased retirement beginning July 31, 2026. Migrate your blueprint definitions and assignments to Azure Deployment Stacks (recommended) and template specs before the retirement date.

notes.front: A building society wants a single map of where sensitive customer data sits across Azure, its own databases on premises and another cloud provider. Which Microsoft offering fits?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Policy
B) A resource lock
C) Microsoft Purview
notes.back: C: Microsoft Purview, through its unified data governance.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: Azure Policy checks Azure resource settings, not where data is held. B is wrong: a lock only stops deletion or changes.
notes.explanation: Purview's unified data governance maps the data estate and identifies where sensitive data is stored, across on-premises and multicloud data.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the purpose of Microsoft Purview, “Unified data governance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A policy allowing only two regions is assigned to a management group. Months later, a developer creates a storage account in a subscription beneath that group. Does the policy apply to it?
notes.choices:
A) No: policies apply only to the management group itself
B) No: policies apply only to resources that existed when assigned
C) Yes: the assignment covers every resource in its scope
notes.back: C: yes, it covers every resource in its scope.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the assignment covers all resources in its scope, not only those present when it was made. A is wrong: the assignment applies to the resources within the scope, not just the group.
notes.explanation: Assignments flow down to all resources in scope, and creating a resource there triggers an evaluation.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “Overview”
notes.evidence: The assignment applies to all resources within the Resource Manager scope of that assignment.

notes.front: A council adopts a new configuration standard, but hundreds of its existing resources were built before it. The team wants them brought into line in bulk, not one by one. What should it use?
notes.choices:
A) A ReadOnly lock on each resource group
B) Azure Policy with remediation
C) A budget with alerts
notes.back: B: Azure Policy with remediation.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a lock prevents change rather than bringing resources into line. C is wrong: a budget tracks spending, not configuration.
notes.explanation: Azure Policy offers bulk remediation for existing resources and automatic remediation for new ones.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “What is Azure Policy?”
notes.evidence: It also helps to bring your resources to compliance through bulk remediation for existing resources and automatic remediation for new resources.

notes.front: A security team has 40 related policy definitions that together meet one compliance goal, and wants to assign and track them as a single item. What should it create?
notes.choices:
A) A policy initiative
B) A resource lock
C) A 41st policy definition
notes.back: A: a policy initiative.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a lock prevents deletion or changes and doesn't group policies. C is wrong: another definition would still leave 41 separate items.
notes.explanation: An initiative groups policy definitions aimed at one overarching goal so they can be managed and assigned as one.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “Initiative definition”
notes.evidence: Initiative definitions simplify managing and assigning policy definitions. They simplify by grouping a set of policies as one single item.

notes.front: An organisation wants every virtual machine anyone creates to use an approved size, however senior the person creating it. Which tool fits this rule?
notes.choices:
A) Azure role-based access control
B) Azure Policy
C) A CanNotDelete lock
notes.back: B: Azure Policy.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: role-based access control decides who may act, not what the resulting resource must look like. C is wrong: the lock only prevents deletion.
notes.explanation: Azure Policy checks resource state against business rules without regard to who made the change.
notes.source: Azure Policy documentation: Overview of Azure Policy, “Azure Policy and Azure RBAC”
notes.evidence: Azure Policy ensures that resource state is compliant to your business rules without concern for who made the change or who has permission to make a change.

notes.front: One database in a resource group has a Delete lock. An engineer tries to delete the whole resource group to tidy up. What happens?
notes.choices:
A) The whole delete operation is blocked
B) Everything except the locked database is deleted
C) Everything is deleted, because the group itself isn't locked
notes.back: A: the whole delete operation is blocked.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a partial deletion isn't possible. C is wrong: the lock on one resource still blocks deleting its group.
notes.explanation: A Delete lock on any resource in the group stops the group's deletion, even if the group and its other resources are unlocked.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure, “Lock inheritance”
notes.evidence: If you have a **Delete** lock on a resource and attempt to delete its resource group, the feature blocks the whole delete operation. Even if the resource group or other resources in the resource group are unlocked, the deletion doesn't happen. A partial deletion isn't possible.

notes.front: A subscription Owner tries to delete a retired virtual machine and is refused because the machine has a CanNotDelete lock. What must she do?
notes.choices:
A) Assign herself a more powerful role
B) Nothing; Owners can't delete locked resources at all
C) Remove the lock, then delete the machine
notes.back: C: remove the lock, then delete the machine.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: locks apply regardless of role permissions, and she is already Owner. B is wrong: once the lock is removed, she can perform any action her permissions allow.
notes.explanation: Changing a locked resource is a two-step process: remove the lock first, then act.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the purpose of resource locks, “How do I delete or change a locked resource?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A production web app's settings are tuned every week, but the app must never be deleted by accident. Which lock should protect it?
notes.choices:
A) ReadOnly
B) CanNotDelete
C) No lock; a lock would block the weekly changes
notes.back: B: CanNotDelete.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: ReadOnly would also block the weekly updates. C is wrong: CanNotDelete still allows modification.
notes.explanation: CanNotDelete lets authorised users read and modify a resource while preventing its deletion.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure
notes.evidence: **CanNotDelete** means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it.
